name: Abiathar (son of Ahimelech)
title: David's faithful priest and the last descendant of Eli in the priesthood
summary: When Doeg the Edomite massacred the priesthood at Nob on King Saul's orders, Abiathar was the only one who escaped with his life. He brought the ephod—the sacred oracle instrument—with him to David and became his closest priest throughout the long years as a fugitive. Through the ephod, Abiathar sought God's will on David's behalf at critical moments, providing David with divine guidance in strategic decisions. After David became king in Jerusalem, Abiathar served as priest alongside Zadok, and the two represented different priestly lines. During Absalom's rebellion, Abiathar demonstrated his loyalty by remaining in the rebel-controlled capital as David's intelligence contact, with his son Jonathan serving as messenger. In David's final days, however, Abiathar chose the wrong side in the succession struggle by supporting Adonijah, while Zadok supported Solomon. After the change of throne, Abiathar was removed from priestly service and exiled to the Levitical town of Anathoth. The biblical authors understand his downfall as the final fulfillment of God's judgment against the house of Eli, prophesied generations earlier—with Abiathar, the priesthood of the line of Ithamar ceased at Israel's central sanctuary, and Zadok's line of Eleazar took over.

keyEvents.title: Flight from Nob
keyEvents.description: Abiathar was the only one who escaped when Doeg the Edomite killed the priests at Nob on Saul's orders. He fled to David with the ephod.

keyEvents.title: Serving as David's priest
keyEvents.description: Abiathar followed David during his flight from Saul and used the ephod to seek God's will for David in important decisions.

keyEvents.title: Priest in Jerusalem under David
keyEvents.description: Together with Zadok, Abiathar served as a priest during David's reign in Jerusalem. The two priests represented different family lines and served side by side.

keyEvents.title: Loyal during Absalom's rebellion
keyEvents.description: When Absalom rebelled, Abiathar remained loyal to David. Together with Zadok, he sent the ark of the covenant back to Jerusalem and acted as David's contact in the city, where his sons Jonathan and Ahimaaz relayed intelligence.

keyEvents.title: Supported Adonijah
keyEvents.description: When David was old, Abiathar supported Adonijah's claim to the throne, unlike Zadok who supported Solomon.

keyEvents.title: Removed and exiled by Solomon
keyEvents.description: After Solomon became king, Abiathar was removed from the priesthood and exiled to Anathoth. This fulfilled the judgment against the house of Eli that had been prophesied generations earlier.

versions.summary: After Doeg the Edomite carried out the massacre of the priesthood at Nob on King Saul's orders, Abiathar was the only one who escaped with his life. He brought the ephod – the holy oracle device – to David, and thus became his closest priest during his time in exile. By consulting God through the ephod, Abiathar helped David make crucial strategic decisions at key moments. When David established himself as king in Jerusalem, Abiathar served as a priest alongside Zadok. During Absalom's rebellion, he remained loyal and acted as David's intelligence contact within the occupied capital. However, toward the end of David's life, Abiathar sided with Adonijah in the struggle for succession, and when Solomon ascended the throne, he was removed from the priesthood and exiled to Anathoth. The biblical authors interpret this as the final fulfillment of the judgment against the house of Eli – Abiathar was the last priest from the line of Ithamar who served at the center of Israel's worship.

footnotes.text: The name Abiathar (Hebrew: אֶבְיָתָר, 'Evyatar) likely means 'my father is excellent' or 'father of abundance', composed of אָב ('av, 'father') and יֶתֶר (yeter, 'abundance/excellence').

In Mark 2:26, Jesus attributes the bread from God's house to 'when Abiathar was high priest,' even though 1 Samuel 21 mentions Ahimelech as the acting priest. This has been the subject of considerable theological discussion. Possible explanations include that Abiathar was already associated with the sanctuary, that his name is used as a time marker for the more well-known priest, or that father and son were known by different names in various traditions.

Abiathar's exile to Anathoth (1 Kings 2:26) is theologically significant because it fulfills the prophecy from 'the man of God' against the house of Eli in 1 Samuel 2:27-36. Abiathar was a descendant of Eli through the line of Ithamar, and with his removal, the high priesthood passed to Zadok of the line of Eleazar.

Anathoth, the place where Abiathar was exiled, was a Levitical city in the tribe of Benjamin, about 5 km northeast of Jerusalem. The city later became known as the hometown of the prophet Jeremiah (Jer 1:1). Archaeological excavations at Ras el-Kharrube near the modern village of Anata have uncovered traces of settlement from the Iron Age.

Abiathar and Zadok served side by side as priests under David, which may reflect a political-religious compromise. Zadok likely represented the Eleazar line (perhaps linked to Jebusite Jerusalem), while Abiathar represented the Ithamar line and the older Shiloh tradition through Eli.

There is a well-known name confusion in the biblical texts between Abiathar and his father Ahimelech. In some passages (e.g., 2 Sam 8:17; 1 Chron 18:16, 24:3), Abiathar is referred to as the father of Ahimelech, while other passages state the opposite. Rabbinic tradition and modern textual criticism suggest this results from scribal errors in the textual transmission.

The ephod that Abiathar brought with him from Nob was a central tool in Israelite oracle practice. The ephod—possibly a form of priestly garment accompanied by the Urim and Thummim—was used to ask yes-or-no questions of God. Abiathar's possession of the ephod gave David a direct channel for divine guidance, providing him with a significant strategic advantage in his battles against Saul and the Philistines.
